Semi-discrete and Wasserstein-1

This chapter develops three computational consequences of duality. Eliminating one potential gives the semi-dual; for discrete measures, this viewpoint leads to auction algorithms, while a continuous source and discrete target lead to Laguerre-cell geometry. The final part specializes duality to W1\Wass_1W1​, where Lipschitz functions and flow fields replace convex potentials. The material connects auction and network-flow methods Bertsekas, 1992Bertsekas & Eckstein, 1988, computational geometry Aurenhammer et al., 1998Mérigot, 2011Mérigot, 2013, and the Kantorovich--Rubinstein and Beckmann formulations Kantorovich & Rubinstein, 1958Beckmann, 1952.

Semi-dual¶

The semi-dual eliminates one potential by an exact ccc-transform. It preserves concavity while removing the explicit pointwise inequality constraint.

General Measure Semi-dual¶

For arbitrary measures, partial maximization converts the constrained two-potential dual into an unconstrained optimization over one function.

Denote the extended full-dual objective by

E0(f,g):={∫Xf  dα+∫Yg  dβ,(f,g)∈R(c),−∞,otherwise.\mathcal E_0(f,g) \eqdef \begin{cases} \displaystyle \int_\X f\,\d\alpha+\int_\Y g\,\d\beta, & (f,g)\in\Potentials(c),\\ -\infty,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases}E0​(f,g):=⎩⎨⎧​∫X​fdα+∫Y​gdβ,−∞,​(f,g)∈R(c),otherwise.​
(1)

Thus Lc(α,β)=max⁡f,gE0(f,g)\mathcal L_c(\alpha,\beta)=\max_{f,g}\mathcal E_0(f,g)Lc​(α,β)=maxf,g​E0​(f,g). For fixed ggg, feasibility is equivalent to f≤gcˉf\leq g^{\bar c}f≤gcˉ. Since α\alphaα is nonnegative, the largest admissible choice f=gcˉf=g^{\bar c}f=gcˉ maximizes the objective and gives

Lc(α,β)=sup⁡g∈C(Y)E(g),E(g):=E0(gcˉ,g)=sup⁡f∈C(X)E0(f,g)=∫Xgcˉ  dα+∫Yg  dβ.\mathcal L_c(\alpha,\beta) = \sup_{g\in\Cc(\Y)}\mathcal E(g), \qquad \mathcal E(g) \eqdef \mathcal E_0(g^{\bar c},g) = \sup_{f\in\Cc(\X)}\mathcal E_0(f,g) = \int_\X g^{\bar c}\,\d\alpha+\int_\Y g\,\d\beta.Lc​(α,β)=g∈C(Y)sup​E(g),E(g):=E0​(gcˉ,g)=f∈C(X)sup​E0​(f,g)=∫X​gcˉdα+∫Y​gdβ.
(2)

Partial maximization preserves concavity. Moreover, E(g+s)=E(g)\mathcal E(g+s)=\mathcal E(g)E(g+s)=E(g) because (g+s)cˉ=gcˉ−s(g+s)^{\bar c}=g^{\bar c}-s(g+s)cˉ=gcˉ−s and both measures have unit mass. Potentials are therefore defined only up to an additive constant, while the optimization is unconstrained.

For two discrete measures

α=∑i=1naiδxi,β=∑j=1mbjδyj,Cij=c(xi,yj),\alpha=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\delta_{x_i}, \qquad \beta=\sum_{j=1}^m b_j\delta_{y_j}, \qquad \C_{ij}=c(x_i,y_j),α=i=1∑n​ai​δxi​​,β=j=1∑m​bj​δyj​​,Cij​=c(xi​,yj​),

with common total mass MMM, use the same notation for vectors:

LC(a,b)=max⁡g∈RmE(g),E(g)=E0(gCˉ,g)=∑i=1nai(gCˉ)i+∑j=1mbjgj,\mathcal L_{\C}(a,b) = \max_{g\in\mathbb R^m}\mathcal E(g), \qquad \mathcal E(g) = \mathcal E_0(g^{\bar\C},g) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i(g^{\bar\C})_i + \sum_{j=1}^m b_jg_j,LC​(a,b)=g∈Rmmax​E(g),E(g)=E0​(gCˉ,g)=i=1∑n​ai​(gCˉ)i​+j=1∑m​bj​gj​,
(5)

where

(gCˉ)i=min⁡1≤j≤m(Cij−gj).(g^{\bar\C})_i=\min_{1\le j\le m}(\C_{ij}-g_j).(gCˉ)i​=1≤j≤mmin​(Cij​−gj​).
(6)

The function E\mathcal EE is concave, piecewise affine, and invariant under g↦g+s1g\mapsto g+s\mathbf 1g↦g+s1. If ties are resolved by choosing σg(i)∈arg⁡min⁡j(Cij−gj)\sigma_g(i)\in\arg\min_j(\C_{ij}-g_j)σg​(i)∈argminj​(Cij​−gj​), then a supergradient is

b−b^(g),b^j(g)=∑i: σg(i)=jai.b-\widehat b(g), \qquad \widehat b_j(g)=\sum_{i:\,\sigma_g(i)=j}a_i.b−b(g),bj​(g)=i:σg​(i)=j∑​ai​.

It is therefore the mismatch between the desired target mass and the mass currently attracted by each target coordinate. At ties, splitting source mass among active targets describes the full superdifferential.

Auction Algorithm¶

The auction algorithm is derived from coordinate maximization of the semi-dual of the linear assignment problem. Its practical form uses bidder-specific dual-weight updates that cross the selected row’s next indifference threshold by ε\varepsilonε; this controlled relaxation prevents jamming at nonsmooth ties. We follow the account of Mérigot and Thibert Mérigot & Thibert, 2020, itself based on Bertsekas’ auction algorithm and its ε\varepsilonε-scaling refinement Bertsekas, 1981Bertsekas & Eckstein, 1988Bertsekas, 1992. In this section, C∈Rn×n\C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}C∈Rn×n and n≥2n\ge2n≥2. A permutation matrix PPP represents the probability coupling P/nP/nP/n.

Coordinate Ascent and Discrete Laguerre Cells¶

Write gjg_jgj​ for the target Kantorovich potential. Specializing the discrete semi-dual to uniform weights gives

E(g)=1n∑i=1n(gCˉ)i+1n∑j=1ngj,(gCˉ)i=min⁡1≤j≤n(Cij−gj).\mathcal E(g) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(g^{\bar\C})_i+\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n g_j, \qquad (g^{\bar\C})_i=\min_{1\le j\le n}(\C_{ij}-g_j).E(g)=n1​i=1∑n​(gCˉ)i​+n1​j=1∑n​gj​,(gCˉ)i​=1≤j≤nmin​(Cij​−gj​).
(8)

Thus (gCˉ,g)(g^{\bar\C},g)(gCˉ,g) is dual feasible. This is the discrete Cˉ\bar CCˉ-transform of Remark Remark: Discrete ccc-transform, with the same sign convention as in the general and semi-discrete formulations.

The discrete Laguerre cells are

Lag⁡jD(g)={i: Cij−gj≤Cik−gk for every k}.\operatorname{Lag}^{\mathrm D}_j(g) = \left\{i:\ \C_{ij}-g_j\le \C_{ik}-g_k\ \text{for every }k\right\}.LagjD​(g)={i: Cij​−gj​≤Cik​−gk​ for every k}.
(9)

They can overlap at ties. They are the finite counterparts of the general semi-discrete Laguerre cells in Definition Definition: Laguerre Cells and Power Diagrams: the displayed cell is that definition restricted to row indices. If every row has a unique minimizer, then

∂∂gjE(g)=1−∣Lag⁡jD(g)∣n.\frac{\partial}{\partial g_j}\mathcal E(g) = \frac{1-|\operatorname{Lag}^{\mathrm D}_j(g)|}{n}.∂gj​∂​E(g)=n1−∣LagjD​(g)∣​.
(10)

An overfull cell therefore calls for a decrease of its dual weight. Proposition Proposition: Dual Certificate for an Assignment shows that a perfect matching in the contact graph i∈Lag⁡jD(g)i\in\operatorname{Lag}^{\mathrm D}_j(g)i∈LagjD​(g) certifies optimality of ggg; conversely, assignment duality and complementary slackness produce such a matching at every maximizer.

For i∈Lag⁡jD(g)i\in\operatorname{Lag}^{\mathrm D}_j(g)i∈LagjD​(g), define

bid⁡j(g,i)=min⁡k≠j(Cik−gk)−(Cij−gj).\operatorname{bid}_j(g,i) = \min_{k\ne j}(\C_{ik}-g_k)-(\C_{ij}-g_j).bidj​(g,i)=k=jmin​(Cik​−gk​)−(Cij​−gj​).
(11)

When the cell is nonempty, the largest maximizing decrement along the negative jjjth coordinate is the largest such bid Mérigot & Thibert, 2020. At a tie, even this largest maximizing decrement can vanish, so naive coordinate ascent may jam before reaching a dual maximizer.

Bids and Relaxed Contacts¶

Auction avoids jamming by moving an unassigned row ε\varepsilonε beyond its next indifference point. Let j0j_0j0​ and j1j_1j1​ be its best and second-best targets:

j0∈arg⁡min⁡j(Cij−gj),j1∈arg⁡min⁡j≠j0(Cij−gj).j_0\in\arg\min_j(\C_{ij}-g_j), \qquad j_1\in\arg\min_{j\ne j_0}(\C_{ij}-g_j).j0​∈argjmin​(Cij​−gj​),j1​∈argj=j0​min​(Cij​−gj​).
(12)

The winning dual weight is updated by

Δi=bid⁡j0(g,i)+ε=(Ci,j1−gj1)−(Ci,j0−gj0)+ε,gj0←gj0−Δi.\Delta_i = \operatorname{bid}_{j_0}(g,i)+\varepsilon = (\C_{i,j_1}-g_{j_1})-(\C_{i,j_0}-g_{j_0})+\varepsilon, \qquad g_{j_0}\leftarrow g_{j_0}-\Delta_i.Δi​=bidj0​​(g,i)+ε=(Ci,j1​​−gj1​​)−(Ci,j0​​−gj0​​)+ε,gj0​​←gj0​​−Δi​.
(13)

Unlike exact coordinate maximization, this update uses the selected row’s bid rather than the maximum bid over the whole cell. Afterward, the reduced cost of j0j_0j0​ is exactly ε\varepsilonε above that of the unchanged alternative j1j_1j1​. The row nevertheless takes j0j_0j0​; its former owner, if any, becomes unassigned. Because of this overshoot, a bid need not increase the nonsmooth semi-dual. Coordinate ascent motivates the update, but ε\varepsilonε-complementary slackness is the invariant used in the convergence proof.

Definition: ε\varepsilonε-Complementary Slackness

A partial permutation matrix P∈{0,1}n×nP\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}P∈{0,1}n×n has at most one nonzero entry in each row and column. Such a matrix and target potential ggg satisfy ε\varepsilonε-complementary slackness if

Pij=1⟹Cij−gj≤(gCˉ)i+ε.P_{ij}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \C_{ij}-g_j\le(g^{\bar\C})_i+\varepsilon.Pij​=1⟹Cij​−gj​≤(gCˉ)i​+ε.
(14)

A bid gives the newly assigned row this property. Decreasing gj0g_{j_0}gj0​​ can only make j0j_0j0​ less attractive to rows assigned elsewhere, and the previous owner of j0j_0j0​ is removed. Every iteration therefore preserves the condition.

Algorithm: Bertsekas Auction

Output: Permutation matrix PPP and target potential ggg; the source potential is gCˉg^{\bar\C}gCˉ.

Initialize: Set P=0P=0P=0.

While some row iii satisfies ∑jPij=0\sum_jP_{ij}=0∑j​Pij​=0 do:

Choose any such row iii.

Set j0∈arg⁡min⁡j(Cij−gj)j_0\in\arg\min_j(\C_{ij}-g_j)j0​∈argminj​(Cij​−gj​) and j1∈arg⁡min⁡j≠j0(Cij−gj)j_1\in\arg\min_{j\ne j_0}(\C_{ij}-g_j)j1​∈argminj=j0​​(Cij​−gj​).

Set Δ←(Ci,j1−gj1)−(Ci,j0−gj0)+ε\Delta\leftarrow(\C_{i,j_1}-g_{j_1})-(\C_{i,j_0}-g_{j_0})+\varepsilonΔ←(Ci,j1​​−gj1​​)−(Ci,j0​​−gj0​​)+ε.

Set Pi,j0←1P_{i,j_0}\leftarrow1Pi,j0​​←1.

Fixed Tolerance¶

For a prescribed tolerance, relaxed contact gives both an optimality certificate and a finite bound on the number of bids.

Proposition: Fixed-ε\varepsilonε Auction Convergence and Complexity

Set RC=max⁡i,jCij−min⁡i,jCijR_{\C}=\max_{i,j}\C_{ij}-\min_{i,j}\C_{ij}RC​=maxi,j​Cij​−mini,j​Cij​. Started from g=0g=0g=0, Algorithm Algorithm: Bertsekas Auction terminates after at most

n(⌊RC/ε⌋+1)n\left(\left\lfloor R_{\C}/\varepsilon\right\rfloor+1\right)n(⌊RC​/ε⌋+1)
(16)

bids. It returns a permutation matrix satisfying ε\varepsilonε-complementary slackness and

0≤1n⟨C,P⟩−min⁡P′∈Pnperm1n⟨C,P′⟩≤ε.0 \le \frac1n\langle\C,P\rangle - \min_{P'\in\mathcal P_n^{\mathrm{perm}}}\frac1n\langle\C,P'\rangle \le \varepsilon.0≤n1​⟨C,P⟩−P′∈Pnperm​min​n1​⟨C,P′⟩≤ε.
(17)

Dense scans require O(n2(1+RC/ε))O(n^2(1+R_{\C}/\varepsilon))O(n2(1+RC​/ε)) operations and O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) storage. If C\CC is integer-valued and ε<1/n\varepsilon<1/nε<1/n, the assignment is exactly optimal.

Proof

Each bid decreases one target potential by at least ε\varepsilonε. Once a target has an owner, later bids may change that owner but never leave the target empty. While the algorithm is incomplete, an unassigned target therefore retains its initial zero potential. A selected target is either unassigned, hence has zero potential, or has value at least −RC-R_{\C}−RC​ by comparison with a zero-potential target. Each target can consequently receive at most ⌊RC/ε⌋+1\lfloor R_{\C}/\varepsilon\rfloor+1⌊RC​/ε⌋+1 bids. At termination every row and column has one active entry.

For the cost certificate, summing ε\varepsilonε-complementary slackness over the returned permutation gives the first inequality below. The second is the dual lower bound of Proposition Proposition: Dual Certificate for an Assignment, applied to (gCˉ,g)(g^{\bar\C},g)(gCˉ,g):

1n⟨C,P⟩≤1n∑i(gCˉ)i+1n∑jgj+ε≤min⁡P′1n⟨C,P′⟩+ε.\frac1n\langle\C,P\rangle \le \frac1n\sum_i(g^{\bar\C})_i+\frac1n\sum_jg_j+\varepsilon \le \min_{P'}\frac1n\langle\C,P'\rangle+\varepsilon.n1​⟨C,P⟩≤n1​i∑​(gCˉ)i​+n1​j∑​gj​+ε≤P′min​n1​⟨C,P′⟩+ε.
(18)

One dense bid scans nnn reduced costs, proving the complexity bound. For integer costs, the unnormalized assignment gap is an integer smaller than one and must therefore vanish.

ε\varepsilonε-Scaling¶

The cold-start estimate above exposes the limitation of a single tolerance. A large ε\varepsilonε is fast but gives only a coarse certificate, whereas the small ε\varepsilonε required for high accuracy can produce a bid count proportional to RC/εR_{\C}/\varepsilonRC​/ε. Continuation first learns a rough dual-potential landscape and then sharpens it instead of restarting from zero.

Algorithm Algorithm: Auction With ε\varepsilonε-Scaling starts at the cost scale max⁡{RC,η}\max\{R_{\C},\eta\}max{RC​,η} and halves the tolerance until it reaches the requested value η\etaη. Each phase rebuilds the ownership matrix but retains the target potential from the preceding phase. The previous complete assignment already certifies approximate contact for this potential, so the next auction refines an existing dual landscape.

Algorithm: Auction With ε\varepsilonε-Scaling

Input: Cost matrix C∈Rn×n\C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}C∈Rn×n, final tolerance η>0\eta>0η>0.

Output: Permutation matrix PPP and target potential ggg; the source potential is gCˉg^{\bar\C}gCˉ.

Initialize: Set RC←max⁡i,jCij−min⁡i,jCijR_{\C}\leftarrow\max_{i,j}\C_{ij}-\min_{i,j}\C_{ij}RC​←maxi,j​Cij​−mini,j​Cij​ and g←0g\leftarrow0g←0.

If RC=0R_{\C}=0RC​=0 then, return any permutation matrix and g=0g=0g=0.

Set ε←max⁡{RC,η}\varepsilon\leftarrow\max\{R_{\C},\eta\}ε←max{RC​,η}.

While ε>η\varepsilon>\etaε>η do:

Set (P,g)←Auction⁡(C,ε,g)(P,g)\leftarrow\operatorname{Auction}(\C,\varepsilon,g)(P,g)←Auction(C,ε,g).

Set ε←max⁡{ε/2,η}\varepsilon\leftarrow\max\{\varepsilon/2,\eta\}ε←max{ε/2,η}.

Set (P,g)←Auction⁡(C,η,g)(P,g)\leftarrow\operatorname{Auction}(\C,\eta,g)(P,g)←Auction(C,η,g).

Return PPP and ggg.

Proposition: Complexity of ε\varepsilonε-Scaling

For η>0\eta>0η>0, Algorithm Algorithm: Auction With ε\varepsilonε-Scaling returns a permutation satisfying η\etaη-complementary slackness and (17) with ε\varepsilonε replaced by η\etaη. If RC>0R_{\C}>0RC​>0, it uses at most

1+⌈log⁡2+ ⁣(RCη)⌉,log⁡2+(s)=max⁡{0,log⁡2s},1+\left\lceil\log_2^+\!\left(\frac{R_{\C}}{\eta}\right)\right\rceil, \qquad \log_2^+(s)=\max\{0,\log_2 s\},1+⌈log2+​(ηRC​​)⌉,log2+​(s)=max{0,log2​s},
(19)

auction phases. Its dense worst-case complexity is

O ⁣(n3(1+log⁡+RCη)),log⁡+(s)=max⁡{0,log⁡s}.O\!\left(n^3\left(1+\log_+\frac{R_{\C}}{\eta}\right)\right), \qquad \log_+(s)=\max\{0,\log s\}.O(n3(1+log+​ηRC​​)),log+​(s)=max{0,logs}.
(20)

If RC=0R_{\C}=0RC​=0, it terminates immediately. For integer-valued C\CC and η<1/n\eta<1/nη<1/n, its output is exactly optimal.

Proof

The initial tolerance is ε0=max⁡{RC,η}\varepsilon_0=\max\{R_{\C},\eta\}ε0​=max{RC​,η}. If it equals η\etaη, the fixed-tolerance proposition gives the result in one phase. Otherwise the first phase starts from the zero potential and costs O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) because RC/ε0=1R_{\C}/\varepsilon_0=1RC​/ε0​=1.

Consider a later ε\varepsilonε-phase initialized from a target potential obtained at preceding tolerance λ\lambdaλ. The preceding assignment satisfies λ\lambdaλ-complementary slackness. Lemma 25 of Mérigot and Thibert Mérigot & Thibert, 2020, expressed in the present sign convention, bounds the decrease of each potential component during the new phase by n(λ+ε)n(\lambda+\varepsilon)n(λ+ε). Since each bid decreases one component by at least ε\varepsilonε, the phase uses at most

n2(1+λε)n^2\left(1+\frac{\lambda}{\varepsilon}\right)n2(1+ελ​)
(21)

bids. Consecutive tolerances satisfy λ/ε≤2\lambda/\varepsilon\leq2λ/ε≤2, hence each warm-started phase costs O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) dense operations. Halving gives the stated phase count. The last phase enforces η\etaη-complementary slackness, so the fixed-tolerance proposition yields the accuracy and integer-cost conclusions.

A cold-started η\etaη-auction has bound O(n2(1+RC/η))O(n^2(1+R_{\C}/\eta))O(n2(1+RC​/η)), while scaling uses a logarithmic number of O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) phases. Thus scaling is a high-accuracy guarantee, not an unconditional speedup: its bound improves the cold-start estimate when RC/ηR_{\C}/\etaRC​/η is large compared with n(1+log⁡+(RC/η))n(1+\log_+(R_{\C}/\eta))n(1+log+​(RC​/η)). For integer costs, choosing η<1/n\eta<1/nη<1/n gives an exact assignment in O(n3(1+log⁡+(nRC)))O(n^3(1+\log_+(nR_{\C})))O(n3(1+log+​(nRC​))) operations.

ε\varepsilonε-Scaling Versus Sinkhorn

Sinkhorn’s continuation parameter has a different role. Entropy smooths the hard minimum into a log-sum-exp, whereas auction retains the hard transform and relaxes only the contact condition. Sinkhorn evolves a dense coupling; auction maintains a partial permutation matrix through dual-weight bids and ownership changes.

Semi-discrete¶

The semi-discrete case is the setting where dual potentials become weights of Laguerre cells. This gives both geometry and algorithms for quantization and density fitting.

Discrete Targets and Laguerre Cells¶

Consider the case where

β=∑j=1mbjδyj\beta=\sum_{j=1}^m b_j\delta_{y_j}β=j=1∑m​bj​δyj​​
(22)

has distinct atoms and positive weights; zero-weight atoms can be removed. The same construction applies if α\alphaα is discrete, after exchanging the roles of α\alphaα and β\betaβ. Restricting the minimization in Definition Definition: ccc-Transform to the support of β\betaβ, equivalently applying that definition with the discrete target space Y={yj}j=1m\Y=\{y_j\}_{j=1}^mY={yj​}j=1m​ and identifying a vector g∈Rmg\in\RR^mg∈Rm with the function g:Y→Rg:\Y\to\RRg:Y→R defined by g(yj)=gjg(y_j)=g_jg(yj​)=gj​, gives the discrete cˉ\bar ccˉ-transform

gcˉ(x):=min⁡1≤j≤mc(x,yj)−gj.g^{\bar c}(x) \eqdef \min_{1\le j\le m} c(x,y_j)-g_j.gcˉ(x):=1≤j≤mmin​c(x,yj​)−gj​.
(23)

This maps a vector ggg to a continuous function because it is the minimum of finitely many continuous functions. Using this transform when β\betaβ is discrete yields the finite-dimensional semi-dual

Lc(α,β)=max⁡g∈RmE(g):=E0(gcˉ,g)=∫Xgcˉ(x)  dα(x)+∑j=1mgjbj.\mathcal{L}_c(\alpha,\beta) = \max_{g\in\RR^m} \mathcal{E}(g) \eqdef \mathcal E_0(g^{\bar c},g) = \int_\X g^{\bar c}(x)\,\d\alpha(x) + \sum_{j=1}^m g_j b_j .Lc​(α,β)=g∈Rmmax​E(g):=E0​(gcˉ,g)=∫X​gcˉ(x)dα(x)+j=1∑m​gj​bj​.
(24)

The objective is invariant under g↦g+s1g\mapsto g+s\mathbf 1g↦g+s1, so one may impose the gauge ∑jgj=0\sum_j g_j=0∑j​gj​=0.

The geometric object encoded by the dual weights is a weighted nearest-neighbor diagram: each source point is assigned to the target atom that realizes the discrete cˉ\bar ccˉ-transform.

Definition: Laguerre Cells and Power Diagrams

For sites (yj)j=1m(y_j)_{j=1}^m(yj​)j=1m​ and weights g∈Rmg\in\RR^mg∈Rm, the Laguerre cell associated with yjy_jyj​ is

Lj(g):={x∈X:c(x,yj)−gj≤c(x,yj′)−gj′for all j′≠j}.\mathcal{L}_j(g) \eqdef \left\{ x\in\X : c(x,y_j)-g_j \le c(x,y_{j'})-g_{j'} \quad\text{for all }j'\ne j \right\}.Lj​(g):={x∈X:c(x,yj​)−gj​≤c(x,yj′​)−gj′​for all j′=j}.
(25)

The cells cover X\XX; after arbitrary tie-breaking on common boundaries, they induce a disjoint partition. When c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2, this decomposition is also called a power diagram. If ggg is constant, it reduces to the ordinary Voronoi diagram.

For quadratic costs, varying the dual weights moves the walls between adjacent cells while keeping them parallel. This is the geometric mechanism by which the cell masses are adjusted.

Figure Div follows this adjustment from unweighted Voronoi cells to a power diagram whose cell masses match the prescribed discrete target weights.

show_book_figure("semidiscrete-laguerre-cells")

Laguerre cells for semi-discrete quadratic transport. The red contours show a continuous source density α\alphaα given by a three-component Gaussian mixture on the right. The twenty-one colored circular sites are the atoms of the discrete target β\betaβ, sampled from a compact cloud on the left; each site color matches its Laguerre cell. Starting from ordinary Voronoi cells, semi-dual weight updates deform the cells so that the α\alphaα-mass captured by each cell approaches the prescribed target mass.

The interactive demo exposes the dual-weight mechanism directly. Increase the number of weight updates to watch cells with too little mass expand and cells with too much mass shrink.

Mass Balance¶

The semi-dual energy can be rewritten as

E(g)=∑j=1m∫Lj(g)(c(x,yj)−gj)  dα(x)+⟨g,b⟩.\mathcal{E}(g) = \sum_{j=1}^m \int_{\mathcal{L}_j(g)} \left(c(x,y_j)-g_j\right)\,\d\alpha(x) + \langle g,b\rangle .E(g)=j=1∑m​∫Lj​(g)​(c(x,yj​)−gj​)dα(x)+⟨g,b⟩.
(26)
Proposition: Gradient of the Semi-discrete Dual

If the minimizing index in the discrete cˉ\bar ccˉ-transform is unique for α\alphaα-almost every xxx, then E\mathcal{E}E is differentiable at ggg and

∂E∂gj(g)=bj−∫Lj(g) dα.\frac{\partial \mathcal{E}}{\partial g_j}(g) = b_j-\int_{\mathcal{L}_j(g)}\d\alpha .∂gj​∂E​(g)=bj​−∫Lj​(g)​dα.
(27)
Proof

For α\alphaα-almost every xxx, the minimizing index in min⁡jc(x,yj)−gj\min_j c(x,y_j)-g_jminj​c(x,yj​)−gj​ is unique. If this index is j(x)j(x)j(x), then the directional derivative in direction h∈Rmh\in\RR^mh∈Rm is

 d dt∣t=0min⁡j(c(x,yj)−gj−thj)=−hj(x).\left.\frac{\d}{\d t}\right|_{t=0} \min_j\left(c(x,y_j)-g_j-t h_j\right) = -h_{j(x)}.dtd​∣∣​t=0​jmin​(c(x,yj​)−gj​−thj​)=−hj(x)​.
(28)

The difference quotients are bounded by ∥h∥∞\norm{h}_\infty∥h∥∞​, so dominated convergence gives

 dE(g)[h]=−∑jhj∫Lj(g) dα+∑jhjbj,\d\mathcal{E}(g)[h] = -\sum_j h_j\int_{\mathcal{L}_j(g)}\d\alpha + \sum_j h_j b_j,dE(g)[h]=−j∑​hj​∫Lj​(g)​dα+j∑​hj​bj​,
(29)

which is the announced gradient formula.

The first-order optimality condition says that solving the semi-discrete dual amounts to choosing weights ggg so that

∫Lj(g) dα=bjfor every j.\int_{\mathcal{L}_j(g)}\d\alpha=b_j \qquad\text{for every }j.∫Lj​(g)​dα=bj​for every j.
(30)

The gradient components sum to zero, consistently with the gauge invariance. Conversely, balanced cells define the piecewise-constant map T(x)=yjT(x)=y_jT(x)=yj​ on Lj(g)\mathcal{L}_j(g)Lj​(g). Its graph lies in the contact set gcˉ(x)+gj=c(x,yj)g^{\bar c}(x)+g_j=c(x,y_j)gcˉ(x)+gj​=c(x,yj​), so continuous complementary slackness proves that both the map and the weights are optimal. For the quadratic cost, uniqueness follows from Brenier’s theorem when α\alphaα has a density.

The sign of the gradient has a direct geometric interpretation. Increasing gjg_jgj​ lowers the corresponding power distance and expands Lj(g)\mathcal L_j(g)Lj​(g); decreasing gjg_jgj​ shrinks it. The dotted outline marks the balanced cell, so semi-dual ascent can be read as a mass-balancing procedure on a power diagram.

Figure Div makes the sign of this gradient geometric.

show_book_figure("semidiscrete-weight-gradient-cells", width=760)

Dual weights control Laguerre cell masses in the semi-discrete quadratic problem. The same blue target sites and red Gaussian source density are used in all panels; only the highlighted violet weight is changed. The dotted violet outline is the balanced cell. If the highlighted cell has too little source mass, then bj−α(Lj(g))>0b_j-\alpha(\mathcal L_j(g))>0bj​−α(Lj​(g))>0 and the ascent update increases the weight, expanding the cell outward. If it has too much mass, the update decreases the weight, shrinking it inward. At balance, the cell mass matches the prescribed target mass and the first-order update vanishes.

Interactive panel. Vary the target weights and the number of dual updates to watch Laguerre cells rebalance their masses.

Quadratic power diagrams have polyhedral cells and can be computed efficiently using computational-geometry algorithms Aurenhammer, 1987Aurenhammer et al., 1998Mérigot, 2011. Expanding the cost shows that a cell minimizes x↦−2⟨x,yj⟩+∥yj∥2−gjx\mapsto-2\langle x,y_j\rangle+\norm{y_j}^2-g_jx↦−2⟨x,yj​⟩+∥yj​∥2−gj​. The lower envelope of these affine functions gives the power diagram, while the lower hull of the lifted sites (yj,∥yj∥2−gj)(y_j,\norm{y_j}^2-g_j)(yj​,∥yj​∥2−gj​) gives its dual regular triangulation. For a planar source, this is a three-dimensional hull and Chan’s output-sensitive algorithm costs O(mlog⁡Q)O(m\log Q)O(mlogQ) for QQQ hull vertices Chan, 1996. A three-dimensional source lifts to four dimensions and is not covered by that particular bound.

Stochastic Optimization¶

The semi-discrete formulation is useful because the objective is an expectation with respect to α\alphaα:

E(g)=∫XE(g,x)  dα(x)=EX(E(g,X)),E(g,x):=gcˉ(x)+⟨g,b⟩.\mathcal{E}(g) = \int_\X E(g,x)\,\d\alpha(x) = \EE_X(E(g,X)), \qquad E(g,x)\eqdef g^{\bar c}(x)+\langle g,b\rangle .E(g)=∫X​E(g,x)dα(x)=EX​(E(g,X)),E(g,x):=gcˉ(x)+⟨g,b⟩.
(31)

Away from cell boundaries, the stochastic gradient of the integrand is

∇gE(g,x)=(bj−1Lj(g)(x))j=1m,\nabla_g E(g,x) = \left(b_j-\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{L}_j(g)}(x)\right)_{j=1}^m,∇g​E(g,x)=(bj​−1Lj​(g)​(x))j=1m​,
(32)

an unbiased estimator of ∇E(g)\nabla\mathcal{E}(g)∇E(g) when cell boundaries have α\alphaα-measure zero. One can therefore maximize the semi-dual without first discretizing α\alphaα: the measure is used as a black box from which independent samples are drawn, a natural setup in high-dimensional statistics and machine learning.

Starting from g(0)=0g^{(0)}=0g(0)=0, stochastic gradient ascent draws xℓ∼αx_\ell\sim\alphaxℓ​∼α and performs

g(ℓ+1):=g(ℓ)+τℓ∇gE(g(ℓ),xℓ).g^{(\ell+1)} \eqdef g^{(\ell)} + \tau_\ell\nabla_g E(g^{(\ell)},x_\ell).g(ℓ+1):=g(ℓ)+τℓ​∇g​E(g(ℓ),xℓ​).
(33)

The stochastic supergradient has zero coordinate sum and preserves the gauge. For almost-sure stochastic-approximation convergence, one typically imposes

∑ℓ=0∞τℓ=∞,∑ℓ=0∞τℓ2<∞.\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\tau_\ell=\infty, \qquad \sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\tau_\ell^2<\infty.ℓ=0∑∞​τℓ​=∞,ℓ=0∑∞​τℓ2​<∞.
(34)

For example, one may use τℓ=τ0(1+ℓ/ℓ0)−q\tau_\ell=\tau_0(1+\ell/\ell_0)^{-q}τℓ​=τ0​(1+ℓ/ℓ0​)−q with 1/2<q≤11/2<q\leq11/2<q≤1. The standard finite-horizon rate instead concerns averaged iterates.

Proposition: Averaged Stochastic Semi-dual Rate

Let g⋆g^\starg⋆ maximize E\mathcal EE, set R=∥g(0)−g⋆∥2R=\norm{g^{(0)}-g^\star}_2R=∥∥​g(0)−g⋆∥∥​2​, and suppose the stochastic supergradients are conditionally unbiased and bounded by GGG. For a horizon LLL, use the constant step τ=R/(GL)\tau=R/(G\sqrt L)τ=R/(GL​) and gˉL=L−1∑ℓ=0L−1g(ℓ)\bar g_L=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}g^{(\ell)}gˉ​L​=L−1∑ℓ=0L−1​g(ℓ). Then

E(g⋆)−E[E(gˉL)]≤RGL.\mathcal{E}(g^\star) - \EE\left[\mathcal{E}(\bar g_L)\right] \leq \frac{RG}{\sqrt L}.E(g⋆)−E[E(gˉ​L​)]≤L​RG​.
(35)
Proof

Concavity and the squared-distance recursion yield

2τ E ⁣[E(g⋆)−E(g(ℓ))]≤E∥g(ℓ)−g⋆∥22−E∥g(ℓ+1)−g⋆∥22+τ2G2.2\tau\,\EE\!\left[\mathcal E(g^\star)-\mathcal E(g^{(\ell)})\right] \leq \EE\norm{g^{(\ell)}-g^\star}_2^2 - \EE\norm{g^{(\ell+1)}-g^\star}_2^2 + \tau^2G^2.2τE[E(g⋆)−E(g(ℓ))]≤E∥∥​g(ℓ)−g⋆∥∥​22​−E∥∥​g(ℓ+1)−g⋆∥∥​22​+τ2G2.
(36)

Summing, discarding the final squared distance, and using concavity at gˉL\bar g_Lgˉ​L​ gives E(g⋆)−EE(gˉL)≤R2/(2τL)+τG2/2\mathcal E(g^\star)-\EE\mathcal E(\bar g_L) \le R^2/(2\tau L)+\tau G^2/2E(g⋆)−EE(gˉ​L​)≤R2/(2τL)+τG2/2. Substitution of τ=R/(GL)\tau=R/(G\sqrt L)τ=R/(GL​) proves the claim.

This stochastic viewpoint is one of the main algorithmic advantages of the semi-discrete formulation Mérigot, 2011Genevay et al., 2016.

Algorithm: Semi-discrete Laguerre Ascent

Input: Source measure α\alphaα, target atoms (yj,bj)(y_j,\b_j)(yj​,bj​), cost ccc, steps (τk)k=0K−1(\tau_k)_{k=0}^{K-1}(τk​)k=0K−1​, tolerance tol\mathrm{tol}tol, maximum iteration count KKK.

Initialize: Set g(0)=0\gD^{(0)}=0g(0)=0.

For k=0,…,K−1k=0,\ldots,K-1k=0,…,K−1 do:

Compute cells: Lj(g(k))={x  :  c(x,yj)−gj(k)≤c(x,yℓ)−gℓ(k)∀ℓ}.\Laguerre_j(\gD^{(k)}) = \enscond{x}{c(x,y_j)-\gD^{(k)}_j\leq c(x,y_\ell)-\gD^{(k)}_\ell\quad\forall \ell}.Lj​(g(k))={x:c(x,yj​)−gj(k)​≤c(x,yℓ​)−gℓ(k)​∀ℓ}.

Compute masses: mj(k)=∫Lj(g(k)) dα.m_j^{(k)}=\int_{\Laguerre_j(\gD^{(k)})}\d\al .mj(k)​=∫Lj​(g(k))​dα.

If max⁡j∣mj(k)−bj∣≤tol\max_j\abs{m_j^{(k)}-\b_j}\leq\mathrm{tol}maxj​∣∣​mj(k)​−bj​∣∣​≤tol then:

Return g(k)\gD^{(k)}g(k) and the current cells.

Update g(k+1)=g(k)+τk(b−m(k)).\gD^{(k+1)} = \gD^{(k)}+\tau_k\bigl(\b-m^{(k)}\bigr).g(k+1)=g(k)+τk​(b−m(k)).

Compute the cells of g(K)\gD^{(K)}g(K).

Return g(K)\gD^{(K)}g(K) and these cells.

Algorithm: Stochastic semi-discrete ascent

Input: Source sampler x∼αx\sim\alphax∼α, target atoms (yj,bj)(y_j,\b_j)(yj​,bj​), steps (τℓ)ℓ=0L−1(\tau_\ell)_{\ell=0}^{L-1}(τℓ​)ℓ=0L−1​, iteration count LLL.

For ℓ=0,…,L−1\ell=0,\ldots,L-1ℓ=0,…,L−1 do:

Draw xℓ∼αx_\ell\sim\alphaxℓ​∼α.

Set jℓ=min⁡arg min⁡j(c(xℓ,yj)−gj(ℓ))j_\ell=\min\argmin_j\bigl(c(x_\ell,y_j)-\gD_j^{(\ell)}\bigr)jℓ​=minargminj​(c(xℓ​,yj​)−gj(ℓ)​).

For j=1,…,mj=1,\ldots,mj=1,…,m do

gj(ℓ+1)=gj(ℓ)+τℓ(bj−1{j=jℓ}).\gD_j^{(\ell+1)} = \gD_j^{(\ell)} + \tau_\ell\bigl(\b_j-\ones_{\{j=j_\ell\}}\bigr).gj(ℓ+1)​=gj(ℓ)​+τℓ​(bj​−1{j=jℓ​}​).

Return gˉL=L−1∑ℓ=0L−1g(ℓ)\bar\gD_L=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}\gD^{(\ell)}gˉ​L​=L−1∑ℓ=0L−1​g(ℓ).

Optimal Quantization¶

Optimal quantization asks for the best discrete approximation of a measure by mmm codepoints. It is the geometric core of vector quantization, compression and kkk-means clustering.

Free Masses and Prescribed Weights¶

The classical problem optimizes both codepoint positions and their probabilities. For a measure α\alphaα, define

Qm(α):=min⁡Y=(yj)j=1m,  b∈ΔmWp(α,∑j=1mbjδyj).\mathcal{Q}_m(\alpha) \eqdef \min_{Y=(y_j)_{j=1}^m,\;b\in\simplex_m} \Wass_p\left(\alpha,\sum_{j=1}^m b_j\delta_{y_j}\right).Qm​(α):=Y=(yj​)j=1m​,b∈Δm​min​Wp​(α,j=1∑m​bj​δyj​​).
(37)

This problem is classical in approximation theory and information theory Graf & Luschgy, 2000Lloyd, 1982.

The equal-weight case, bj=1/mb_j=1/mbj​=1/m, prescribes the weights and is treated at the end of this section.

Proposition: Quantization Rate and Curse of Dimensionality

Let α\alphaα be supported in a bounded Ω⊂Rd\Omega\subset\RR^dΩ⊂Rd and assume α=ρ  dx\alpha=\rho\,\d xα=ρdx with ρ≤ρ+<+∞\rho\le\rho_+<+\inftyρ≤ρ+​<+∞. Then, for fixed p≥1p\ge1p≥1, there exist constants 0<c≤C<+∞0<c\le C<+\infty0<c≤C<+∞ such that

c m−1/d≤Qm(α)≤C m−1/d.c\,m^{-1/d} \le \mathcal{Q}_m(\alpha) \le C\,m^{-1/d}.cm−1/d≤Qm​(α)≤Cm−1/d.
(38)
Proof

Enclose Ω\OmegaΩ in a cube and subdivide it into kd≤mk^d\le mkd≤m congruent cubes, where k=⌊m1/d⌋k=\lfloor m^{1/d}\rfloork=⌊m1/d⌋. Placing one codepoint in each nonempty cube gives the upper bound.

For the lower bound, fix any set YYY of mmm codepoints and write dY(x)=min⁡j∥x−yj∥d_Y(x)=\min_j\norm{x-y_j}dY​(x)=minj​∥x−yj​∥. Since the density is bounded above, the mass of the ttt-neighborhood of YYY has mass at most ρ+mωdtd\rho_+m\omega_dt^dρ+​mωd​td. For t0=(2ρ+mωd)−1/dt_0=(2\rho_+m\omega_d)^{-1/d}t0​=(2ρ+​mωd​)−1/d, one has α({dY>t})≥1/2\alpha(\{d_Y>t\})\ge1/2α({dY​>t})≥1/2 for 0<t<t00<t<t_00<t<t0​. Hence

∫dY(x)p  dα(x)=∫0+∞ptp−1α({dY>t})  dt≥t0p2≃cm−p/d.\int d_Y(x)^p\,\d\alpha(x) = \int_0^{+\infty} p t^{p-1}\alpha(\{d_Y>t\})\,\d t \ge \frac{t_0^p}{2} \simeq c m^{-p/d}.∫dY​(x)pdα(x)=∫0+∞​ptp−1α({dY​>t})dt≥2t0p​​≃cm−p/d.
(39)

Taking the ppp-th root and minimizing over YYY proves the lower bound.

This deterministic rate mirrors the empirical optimal-transport sample-complexity rate: both are governed by the spacing m−1/dm^{-1/d}m−1/d of points in dimension ddd. Quantization is best-case and deterministic, while empirical OT is random, but both display the same curse of dimensionality. Zador’s theorem further identifies the sharp asymptotic constant and limiting codepoint density Graf & Luschgy, 2000.

For fixed codepoints YYY, the powered cost b↦Wpp(α,∑jbjδyj)b\mapsto\Wass_p^p(\alpha,\sum_jb_j\delta_{y_j})b↦Wpp​(α,∑j​bj​δyj​​) is convex. Its ppp-th root Wp\Wass_pWp​ need not be convex. The dependence on YYY is nonconvex and is generally computationally hard. The rest of this section distinguishes the free-mass Lloyd reduction from the fixed-weight geometry underlying finite-particle W2\mathcal W_2W2​ gradient flows.

Lloyd Algorithm¶

The computational appeal of quantization comes from splitting the nonconvex search over sites into two elementary operations. For fixed sites, the optimal assignment is purely local: each point is sent to one of its nearest sites, and the resulting cells are Voronoi cells. This is the assignment step behind Lloyd’s algorithm and the kkk-means method.

Proposition: Free Masses Give Voronoi Cells

For the cost c(x,y)=d(x,y)pc(x,y)=d(x,y)^pc(x,y)=d(x,y)p, fix distinct codepoints Y=(yj)j=1mY=(y_j)_{j=1}^mY=(yj​)j=1m​. Duplicate codepoints can be merged beforehand. Minimizing over the weights b∈Δmb\in\simplex_mb∈Δm​ gives

min⁡b∈ΔmWpp(α,∑jbjδyj)=∫Xmin⁡1≤j≤mc(x,yj)  dα(x).\min_{b\in\simplex_m} \Wass_p^p \left(\alpha,\sum_j b_j\delta_{y_j}\right) = \int_\X \min_{1\le j\le m} c(x,y_j)\,\d\alpha(x).b∈Δm​min​Wpp​(α,j∑​bj​δyj​​)=∫X​1≤j≤mmin​c(x,yj​)dα(x).
(40)

An optimal coupling is induced by sending each xxx to a nearest codepoint. The corresponding cells are the Voronoi cells

Vj(Y):={x:c(x,yj)≤c(x,yj′)for all j′},\mathcal{V}_j(Y) \eqdef \left\{ x : c(x,y_j)\le c(x,y_{j'}) \quad\text{for all }j' \right\},Vj​(Y):={x:c(x,yj​)≤c(x,yj′​)for all j′},
(41)

up to arbitrary tie-breaking on common boundaries.

Proof

For any coupling between α\alphaα and a measure supported on YYY, the conditional destination of a point xxx belongs to YYY, so its conditional cost is at least min⁡jc(x,yj)\min_j c(x,y_j)minj​c(x,yj​). Integrating gives the lower bound. Conversely, choose a measurable nearest-codepoint map TY(x)∈arg min⁡jc(x,yj)T_Y(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_j c(x,y_j)TY​(x)∈argminj​c(x,yj​), breaking ties measurably, and set bj=α(TY−1(yj))b_j=\alpha(T_Y^{-1}(y_j))bj​=α(TY−1​(yj​)). Then (TY)♯α=∑jbjδyj(T_Y)_\sharp\alpha=\sum_j b_j\delta_{y_j}(TY​)♯​α=∑j​bj​δyj​​ and the induced transport reaches the displayed lower bound.

Consequently, the quantization energy can be written in nearest-centroid form:

Qm(α)p=min⁡YF(Y),F(Y):=∫Xmin⁡1≤j≤mc(x,yj)  dα(x).\mathcal{Q}_m(\alpha)^p = \min_Y \mathcal{F}(Y), \qquad \mathcal{F}(Y) \eqdef \int_\X \min_{1\le j\le m} c(x,y_j)\,\d\alpha(x).Qm​(α)p=Ymin​F(Y),F(Y):=∫X​1≤j≤mmin​c(x,yj​)dα(x).
(42)

At a differentiability point of this energy, any local minimizer with nonempty cells satisfies the centroid condition

yj∈arg min⁡y∫Vj(Y)c(x,y)  dα(x).y_j \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{y} \int_{\mathcal{V}_j(Y)} c(x,y)\,\d\alpha(x).yj​∈yargmin​∫Vj​(Y)​c(x,y)dα(x).
(43)

For the squared Euclidean cost, this becomes

yj=∫Vj(Y)x  dα(x)∫Vj(Y) dα.y_j = \frac{\int_{\mathcal{V}_j(Y)} x\,\d\alpha(x)} {\int_{\mathcal{V}_j(Y)} \d\alpha}.yj​=∫Vj​(Y)​dα∫Vj​(Y)​xdα(x)​.
(44)

Lloyd’s algorithm, also known as the kkk-means algorithm, iterates this fixed point: assign points to nearest sites, then replace each site by the centroid of its cell Lloyd, 1982. The assignment and centroid steps each minimize the appropriate block, so the objective cannot increase. Nonconvexity means this does not guarantee a global minimizer. For a finite data set with squared Euclidean loss, kkk-means++ gives an expected logarithmic approximation guarantee Arthur & Vassilvitskii, 2007.

Continuous Lloyd Flow¶

There is also an infinitesimal version of Lloyd’s fixed point, but it should first be understood on finite labelled configurations. Assume that c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2 and that α\alphaα does not charge Voronoi boundaries. For a configuration YYY, define, on nonempty cells,

aj(Y)=α(Vj(Y)),bj(Y)=1aj(Y)∫Vj(Y)x  dα(x)a_j(Y)=\alpha(\mathcal V_j(Y)), \qquad b_j(Y)=\frac{1}{a_j(Y)} \int_{\mathcal V_j(Y)}x\,\d\alpha(x)aj​(Y)=α(Vj​(Y)),bj​(Y)=aj​(Y)1​∫Vj​(Y)​xdα(x)
(45)

as the cell mass and centroid. Empty cells are singular points of the vector field; one either freezes them, as in the algorithm below, or reseeds them. The relaxed step

yj(k+1)=yj(k)+τ(bj(Y(k))−yj(k)),0<τ≤1,y_j^{(k+1)} = y_j^{(k)}+\tau\big(b_j(Y^{(k)})-y_j^{(k)}\big), \qquad 0<\tau\le 1,yj(k+1)​=yj(k)​+τ(bj​(Y(k))−yj(k)​),0<τ≤1,
(46)

is an explicit-Euler step for the cell-mass preconditioned gradient flow of the quantization energy F\mathcal FF,

y˙j(t)=bj(Yt)−yj(t).\dot y_j(t)=b_j(Y_t)-y_j(t).y˙​j​(t)=bj​(Yt​)−yj​(t).
(47)

Indeed, at differentiability points of F\mathcal FF, the envelope theorem gives

∇yjF(Y)=2∫Vj(Y)(yj−x) dα(x)=2aj(Y)(yj−bj(Y)),\nabla_{y_j}\mathcal F(Y) = 2\int_{\mathcal V_j(Y)}(y_j-x)\d\alpha(x) = 2a_j(Y)(y_j-b_j(Y)),∇yj​​F(Y)=2∫Vj​(Y)​(yj​−x)dα(x)=2aj​(Y)(yj​−bj​(Y)),
(48)

so that

y˙j(t)=−12aj(Yt)∇yjF(Yt).\dot y_j(t) = -\frac{1}{2a_j(Y_t)}\nabla_{y_j}\mathcal F(Y_t).y˙​j​(t)=−2aj​(Yt​)1​∇yj​​F(Yt​).
(49)

Equivalently, this is the gradient flow of F\mathcal FF for the site metric gY(U,V)=2∑jaj(Y)⟨uj,vj⟩g_Y(U,V)=2\sum_j a_j(Y)\langle u_j,v_j\ranglegY​(U,V)=2∑j​aj​(Y)⟨uj​,vj​⟩; it is not the unweighted Euclidean gradient flow unless the masses are absorbed into the time step. Along smooth portions of the flow,

 d dtF(Yt)=−2∑jaj(Yt)∥bj(Yt)−yj(t)∥2≤0.\frac{\d}{\d t}\mathcal F(Y_t) = -2\sum_j a_j(Y_t)\|b_j(Y_t)-y_j(t)\|^2 \le 0.dtd​F(Yt​)=−2j∑​aj​(Yt​)∥bj​(Yt​)−yj​(t)∥2≤0.
(50)

If ηt=∑jwjδyj(t)\eta_t=\sum_j w_j\delta_{y_j(t)}ηt​=∑j​wj​δyj​(t)​ carries fixed positive weights, independent of the Voronoi masses aj(Yt)a_j(Y_t)aj​(Yt​), this labelled particle ODE is equivalently a weak continuity equation,

∂tηt+div⁡(vtηt)=0,vt(yj(t))=bj(Yt)−yj(t),\partial_t\eta_t+\operatorname{div}(v_t\eta_t)=0, \qquad v_t(y_j(t))=b_j(Y_t)-y_j(t),∂t​ηt​+div(vt​ηt​)=0,vt​(yj​(t))=bj​(Yt​)−yj​(t),
(51)

in the sense of the measure evolutions introduced in Chapter Paragraph. The weights wjw_jwj​ in this transport equation are auxiliary weights for the moving labelled particles; they are not the Voronoi masses used to define the quantization energy. If one records instead the free-weight projection

νYt=∑jaj(Yt)δyj(t),\nu_{Y_t}=\sum_j a_j(Y_t)\delta_{y_j(t)},νYt​​=j∑​aj​(Yt​)δyj​(t)​,
(52)

then, formally,

∂tνYt+div⁡(vtνYt)=∑ja˙j(Yt)δyj(t),vt(yj(t))=y˙j(t).\partial_t\nu_{Y_t}+\operatorname{div}(v_t\nu_{Y_t}) = \sum_j\dot a_j(Y_t)\delta_{y_j(t)}, \qquad v_t(y_j(t))=\dot y_j(t).∂t​νYt​​+div(vt​νYt​​)=j∑​a˙j​(Yt​)δyj​(t)​,vt​(yj​(t))=y˙​j​(t).
(53)

Thus the free-weight quantizer evolves by a balance equation, not by pure transport. This is why the construction is intrinsically finite-dimensional: Voronoi cells, centroids and labels define the velocity, and a canonical extension to arbitrary measures is not obtained by replacing YYY with the support of a measure. Indeed, any measure with dense support would have zero support-distance quantization error.

Mean-Field Limit and Ultrafast Diffusion¶

There is nevertheless a precise high-resolution continuum theory when the number mmm of codepoints tends to infinity. If α=ρ  dx\alpha=\rho\,\d xα=ρdx, the limiting Eulerian variable is the density σ\sigmaσ of sites, meaning heuristically that mσ(x)  dxm\sigma(x)\,\d xmσ(x)dx codepoints lie in  dx\d xdx. Thus the limit is m→+∞m\to+\inftym→+∞, not a limit in the exponent of the PDE. In one dimension, Caglioti, Golse and Iacobelli embed the ordered particle configuration in L2(0,1)L^2(0,1)L2(0,1) and prove quantitative convergence of the discrete gradient flow toward a limiting flow Caglioti et al., 2015. A perturbative two-dimensional analysis around the optimal hexagonal lattice is developed in Caglioti et al., 2018. For ppp-quantization in dimension ddd, set r=p/dr=p/dr=p/d, so r=2/dr=2/dr=2/d for the quadratic cost used in this section, and write Fp(Y)=∫min⁡j∥x−yj∥p  dα(x)\mathcal F_p(Y)=\int\min_j\norm{x-y_j}^p\,\d\alpha(x)Fp​(Y)=∫minj​∥x−yj​∥pdα(x). For well-prepared configurations whose empirical site distributions converge to σ  dx\sigma\,\d xσdx, the rescaled energy is described, up to a universal cell-shape constant, by

Gρ(σ):=∫Ωρ(x)σ(x)−r  dx,∫Ωσ  dx=1,\mathcal G_\rho(\sigma) \eqdef \int_\Omega \rho(x) \sigma(x)^{-r}\,\d x, \qquad \int_\Omega \sigma\,\d x=1,Gρ​(σ):=∫Ω​ρ(x)σ(x)−rdx,∫Ω​σdx=1,
(54)

Formally,

mrFp(Y(m))≃Cp,dGρ(σ),mrQm(α)p⟶Cp,dmin⁡σGρ(σ).m^r\mathcal F_p(Y^{(m)})\simeq C_{p,d}\mathcal G_\rho(\sigma), \qquad m^r\mathcal Q_m(\alpha)^p \longrightarrow C_{p,d}\min_\sigma\mathcal G_\rho(\sigma).mrFp​(Y(m))≃Cp,d​Gρ​(σ),mrQm​(α)p⟶Cp,d​σmin​Gρ​(σ).
(55)

Since the first variation is −rρσ−r−1-r\rho\sigma^{-r-1}−rρσ−r−1, the formal W2\mathcal W_2W2​-gradient flow is the weighted ultrafast diffusion equation

∂tσ=−r div⁡ ⁣(σ∇ ⁣(ρσr+1)),\partial_t \sigma = -r\,\operatorname{div}\!\left( \sigma\nabla\!\left(\frac{\rho}{\sigma^{r+1}}\right) \right),∂t​σ=−rdiv(σ∇(σr+1ρ​)),
(56)

with periodic or no-flux boundary conditions. Iacobelli studies the associated one-dimensional very-fast-diffusion equation and its convergence to equilibrium Iacobelli, 2019; Iacobelli, Patacchini and Santambrogio then use the JKO scheme and Wasserstein-gradient-flow tools to prove well-posedness, regularity estimates and convergence for a multidimensional weighted version Iacobelli et al., 2019. When ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0, set ω=ρ1/(r+1)\omega=\rho^{1/(r+1)}ω=ρ1/(r+1) and u=σ/ωu=\sigma/\omegau=σ/ω. The same equation becomes

∂tu=−r+1ωdiv⁡ ⁣(ω∇(u−r)),\partial_t u = -\frac{r+1}{\omega}\operatorname{div}\!\left(\omega\nabla(u^{-r})\right),∂t​u=−ωr+1​div(ω∇(u−r)),
(57)

which makes the negative exponent, hence the ultrafast-diffusion character, explicit. Its stationary site density is proportional to ρd/(d+p)\rho^{d/(d+p)}ρd/(d+p).

Algorithm: Lloyd quantization

Input: Source measure α\alphaα, initial codepoints Y(0)=(yj(0))j=1mY^{(0)}=(y_j^{(0)})_{j=1}^mY(0)=(yj(0)​)j=1m​, squared Euclidean cost, tolerance tol\mathrm{tol}tol, maximum iteration count KKK.

Output: Codepoints Y=(yj)j=1mY=(y_j)_{j=1}^mY=(yj​)j=1m​.

Initialize: Set d0=+∞d_0=+\inftyd0​=+∞ and k=0k=0k=0.

While dk>told_k>\mathrm{tol}dk​>tol and k<Kk<Kk<K do:

Set k←k+1k\leftarrow k+1k←k+1.

Compute Voronoi cells: Vj(Y(k−1))={x  :  c(x,yj(k−1))≤c(x,yℓ(k−1))∀ℓ}.\VV_j(Y^{(k-1)}) = \enscond{x}{c(x,y_j^{(k-1)})\leq c(x,y_\ell^{(k-1)})\quad\forall \ell}.Vj​(Y(k−1))={x:c(x,yj(k−1)​)≤c(x,yℓ(k−1)​)∀ℓ}.

For each nonempty cell Vj\VV_jVj​ do

yj(k)=∫Vj(Y(k−1))x  dα(x)∫Vj(Y(k−1)) dα(x).y_j^{(k)} = \frac{\int_{\VV_j(Y^{(k-1)})}x\,\d\al(x)} {\int_{\VV_j(Y^{(k-1)})}\d\al(x)}.yj(k)​=∫Vj​(Y(k−1))​dα(x)∫Vj​(Y(k−1))​xdα(x)​.

For each empty cell Vj\VV_jVj​ do:

Set yj(k)=yj(k−1)y_j^{(k)}=y_j^{(k-1)}yj(k)​=yj(k−1)​.

Set dk=max⁡j∥yj(k)−yj(k−1)∥d_k=\max_j\norm{y_j^{(k)}-y_j^{(k-1)}}dk​=maxj​∥∥​yj(k)​−yj(k−1)​∥∥​.

Return Y(k)Y^{(k)}Y(k).

Quantization with Fixed Equal Weights¶

The free-mass formulation above optimizes the positions and the weights of the atoms. A different problem is obtained by prescribing the weights. In the equal-weight case, set

νY:=1m∑j=1mδyj,Feq(Y):=12W22(α,νY),\nu_Y\eqdef \frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m\delta_{y_j}, \qquad \mathcal F_{\rm eq}(Y) \eqdef \frac12\mathcal W_2^2(\alpha,\nu_Y),νY​:=m1​j=1∑m​δyj​​,Feq​(Y):=21​W22​(α,νY​),
(58)

and minimize only over the positions Y=(yj)jY=(y_j)_jY=(yj​)j​. Assume that the sites are distinct, that α\alphaα has a density, and that cell boundaries have zero α\alphaα-mass. Let Cj(Y)C_j(Y)Cj​(Y) be the Laguerre cell transported to yjy_jyj​, so that α(Cj(Y))=1/m\alpha(C_j(Y))=1/mα(Cj​(Y))=1/m, and define its centroid

xˉj(Y):=m∫Cj(Y)x  dα(x).\bar x_j(Y) \eqdef m\int_{C_j(Y)} x\,\d\alpha(x).xˉj​(Y):=m∫Cj​(Y)​xdα(x).
(59)

At differentiability points, the envelope theorem gives

∇yjFeq(Y)=1m(yj−xˉj(Y)).\nabla_{y_j}\mathcal F_{\rm eq}(Y) = \frac1m\bigl(y_j-\bar x_j(Y)\bigr).∇yj​​Feq​(Y)=m1​(yj​−xˉj​(Y)).
(60)

Locally, while labels remain optimally matched, the W2\mathcal W_2W2​ metric on equal-weight empirical measures induces the particle metric gY(U,V)=m−1∑j⟨uj,vj⟩g_Y(U,V)=m^{-1}\sum_j\langle u_j,v_j\ranglegY​(U,V)=m−1∑j​⟨uj​,vj​⟩. Hence the associated W2\mathcal W_2W2​ gradient flow is the coupled system

y˙j(t)=xˉj(Yt)−yj(t),j=1,…,m.\dot y_j(t) = \bar x_j(Y_t)-y_j(t), \qquad j=1,\ldots,m.y˙​j​(t)=xˉj​(Yt​)−yj​(t),j=1,…,m.
(61)

Equivalently, νYt\nu_{Y_t}νYt​​ satisfies a continuity equation with velocity vt(yj(t))=xˉj(Yt)−yj(t)v_t(y_j(t))=\bar x_j(Y_t)-y_j(t)vt​(yj​(t))=xˉj​(Yt​)−yj​(t). This is the so-called finite-particle W2\mathcal W_2W2​ gradient-flow viewpoint developed more systematically in Chapter Paragraph; the fixed-weight cells are Laguerre cells rather than the free-mass Voronoi cells used by Lloyd’s method.

Equal-Weight Quantization on the Line¶

The following classical scalar quantization result gives the precise form of the inverse-CDF rule for equal-weight quadratic quantization Graf & Luschgy, 2000. The atoms are not exactly the midpoint quantiles in general; they are the averages of the quantile function over equal mass bins. Midpoint inverse-CDF samples are nevertheless asymptotically equivalent and are often the most convenient rule in numerical examples.

Proposition: One-Dimensional Equal-Weight Quantization

Let α∈M+1(R)\alpha\in\mathcal M_+^1(\mathbb R)α∈M+1​(R) have finite second moment and quantile function Q=Fα−1Q=F_\alpha^{-1}Q=Fα−1​. For

Qm,eq(α)2:=min⁡y1≤⋯≤ymW22(α,1m∑i=1mδyi),\mathcal Q_{m,\mathrm{eq}}(\alpha)^2 \eqdef \min_{y_1\le\cdots\le y_m} \mathcal W_2^2 \left(\alpha,\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_{y_i}\right),Qm,eq​(α)2:=y1​≤⋯≤ym​min​W22​(α,m1​i=1∑m​δyi​​),
(62)

set Ii=((i−1)/m,i/m]I_i=((i-1)/m,i/m]Ii​=((i−1)/m,i/m]. Then the sorted minimizer is unique and its iiith atom is

yi⋆=m∫IiQ(u)  du,y_i^\star = m\int_{I_i} Q(u)\,\d u,yi⋆​=m∫Ii​​Q(u)du,
(63)

and

Qm,eq(α)2=∑i=1m∫Ii∣Q(u)−yi⋆∣2  du.\mathcal Q_{m,\mathrm{eq}}(\alpha)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^m \int_{I_i} \left|Q(u)-y_i^\star\right|^2\,\d u.Qm,eq​(α)2=i=1∑m​∫Ii​​∣Q(u)−yi⋆​∣2du.
(64)

If Q∈C1([0,1])Q\in C^1([0,1])Q∈C1([0,1]), then

m2Qm,eq(α)2⟶112∫01∣Q′(u)∣2  du.m^2\mathcal Q_{m,\mathrm{eq}}(\alpha)^2 \longrightarrow \frac1{12}\int_0^1 |Q'(u)|^2\,\d u.m2Qm,eq​(α)2⟶121​∫01​∣Q′(u)∣2du.
(65)
Proof

After sorting the atoms, the quantile formula for W2\mathcal W_2W2​ gives

W22(α,1m∑i=1mδyi)=∑i=1m∫Ii∣Q(u)−yi∣2  du.\mathcal W_2^2 \left(\alpha,\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_{y_i}\right) = \sum_{i=1}^m \int_{I_i}|Q(u)-y_i|^2\,\d u.W22​(α,m1​i=1∑m​δyi​​)=i=1∑m​∫Ii​​∣Q(u)−yi​∣2du.
(66)

The minimization decouples over the intervals IiI_iIi​, and the best constant approximation of QQQ on IiI_iIi​ is its average. These averages are nondecreasing because QQQ is nondecreasing, so they satisfy the sorting constraint. Strict convexity gives uniqueness.

Denote by QˉIi=m∫IiQ(u)  du\bar Q_{I_i}=m\int_{I_i}Q(u)\,\d uQˉ​Ii​​=m∫Ii​​Q(u)du the interval average. If QQQ is C1C^1C1, set h=1/mh=1/mh=1/m and write Ii=(ai,ai+h]I_i=(a_i,a_i+h]Ii​=(ai​,ai​+h]. Uniform Taylor expansion gives, for v∈[0,1]v\in[0,1]v∈[0,1],

Q(ai+hv)=Q(ai)+hvQ′(ai)+h ri(v),max⁡isup⁡v∈[0,1]∣ri(v)∣→0.Q(a_i+hv) = Q(a_i)+hvQ'(a_i)+h\,r_i(v), \qquad \max_i\sup_{v\in[0,1]} |r_i(v)|\to0.Q(ai​+hv)=Q(ai​)+hvQ′(ai​)+hri​(v),imax​v∈[0,1]sup​∣ri​(v)∣→0.
(67)

Subtracting the average over v∈[0,1]v\in[0,1]v∈[0,1] and integrating gives

∫Ii∣Q(u)−QˉIi∣2  du=h312∣Q′(ai)∣2+o(h3),\int_{I_i}|Q(u)-\bar Q_{I_i}|^2\,\d u = \frac{h^3}{12}|Q'(a_i)|^2+o(h^3),∫Ii​​∣Q(u)−Qˉ​Ii​​∣2du=12h3​∣Q′(ai​)∣2+o(h3),
(68)

uniformly in iii. Summing over iii yields a Riemann sum for 112∫01∣Q′(u)∣2  du\frac1{12}\int_0^1 |Q'(u)|^2\,\d u121​∫01​∣Q′(u)∣2du.

Thus the common deterministic rule m−1∑iδQ((i−1/2)/m)m^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{Q((i-1/2)/m)}m−1∑i​δQ((i−1/2)/m)​ should be read as a midpoint approximation of the optimal bin-average formula. Orthogonal projection onto constants shows that it has the same leading squared error under the same smoothness assumptions; for the uniform law on [0,1][0,1][0,1], both rules coincide and give the regular grid yi=(i−1/2)/my_i=(i-1/2)/myi​=(i−1/2)/m. Random sampling has a different asymptotic regime.

Proposition: Quantile-Process Asymptotics for Random Placement

Let α∈M+1(R)\alpha\in\mathcal M_+^1(\mathbb R)α∈M+1​(R) have quantile Q∈C1([0,1])Q\in C^1([0,1])Q∈C1([0,1]), and let α^m=m−1∑i=1mδXi\widehat\alpha_m=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_{X_i}αm​=m−1∑i=1m​δXi​​ with XiX_iXi​ i.i.d. with law α\alphaα. If BBB denotes the standard Brownian bridge on [0,1][0,1][0,1], then

m W22(α,α^m)⟶law∫01B(u)2∣Q′(u)∣2  du,m\,\mathcal W_2^2(\alpha,\widehat\alpha_m) \overset{\mathrm{law}}{\longrightarrow} \int_0^1 B(u)^2 |Q'(u)|^2\,\d u,mW22​(α,αm​)⟶law​∫01​B(u)2∣Q′(u)∣2du,
(69)

and, in expectation,

m E ⁣[W22(α,α^m)]⟶∫01u(1−u)∣Q′(u)∣2  du.m\,\mathbb E\!\left[ \mathcal W_2^2(\alpha,\widehat\alpha_m) \right] \longrightarrow \int_0^1 u(1-u)|Q'(u)|^2\,\d u.mE[W22​(α,αm​)]⟶∫01​u(1−u)∣Q′(u)∣2du.
(70)
Proof

Let Q^m\widehat Q_mQ​m​ be the empirical quantile function. The one-dimensional formula gives

W22(α,α^m)=∫01∣Q^m(u)−Q(u)∣2  du.\mathcal W_2^2(\alpha,\widehat\alpha_m) = \int_0^1|\widehat Q_m(u)-Q(u)|^2\,\d u.W22​(α,αm​)=∫01​∣Q​m​(u)−Q(u)∣2du.
(71)

Write Xi=Q(Ui)X_i=Q(U_i)Xi​=Q(Ui​) with UiU_iUi​ i.i.d. uniform on [0,1][0,1][0,1], and let U^m−1\widehat U_m^{-1}Um−1​ be the empirical quantile function of the UiU_iUi​. Then Q^m=Q∘U^m−1\widehat Q_m=Q\circ \widehat U_m^{-1}Q​m​=Q∘Um−1​. The classical uniform quantile-process theorem Vaart & Wellner, 1996Bobkov & Ledoux, 2019 gives

m (U^m−1−Id⁡)⟶law−Bin L2(0,1).\sqrt m\,(\widehat U_m^{-1}-\operatorname{Id}) \overset{\mathrm{law}}{\longrightarrow} -B \quad\text{in }L^2(0,1).m​(Um−1​−Id)⟶law​−Bin L2(0,1).
(72)

Uniform continuity of Q′Q'Q′ and the functional delta method give

m (Q^m−Q)⟶law−BQ′in L2(0,1).\sqrt m\,(\widehat Q_m-Q) \overset{\mathrm{law}}{\longrightarrow} -BQ' \quad\text{in }L^2(0,1).m​(Q​m​−Q)⟶law​−BQ′in L2(0,1).
(73)

Since BBB and −B-B−B have the same law, the sign disappears in the squared L2L^2L2 norm. The continuous mapping theorem gives the distributional convergence. Standard fourth-moment bounds for the uniform quantile process give uniform integrability, hence convergence of expectations. Since E[B(u)2]=u(1−u)\mathbb E[B(u)^2]=u(1-u)E[B(u)2]=u(1−u), Fubini’s theorem gives the displayed expectation limit.

Combining these propositions gives a sharp contrast between optimal placement and random placement on the line. Deterministic equal-weight quantization has squared error of order m−2m^{-2}m−2, hence W2\mathcal W_2W2​ error of order m−1m^{-1}m−1, while i.i.d. empirical sampling has expected squared error of order m−1m^{-1}m−1, hence root-mean-square W2\mathcal W_2W2​ error of order m−1/2m^{-1/2}m−1/2. This is consistent with broader empirical OT sample-complexity theory Dereich et al., 2013Fournier & Guillin, 2015Weed & Bach, 2019.

Figure Div illustrates both parts of this comparison: optimal atoms are uniform in quantile coordinates, and their error decays one power of mmm faster than the root-mean-square empirical error.

Wasserstein-1 Norm¶

The W1\Wass_1W1​ distance has an especially transparent dual: the admissible potentials are exactly 1-Lipschitz test functions. This makes W1\Wass_1W1​ the meeting point between transport, PDE formulations and weak norms on signed measures.

c-Transform for Wasserstein-1¶

Assume that ddd is a distance on X=Y\X=\YX=Y and take the ground cost c(x,y)=d(x,y)c(x,y)=d(x,y)c(x,y)=d(x,y).

Definition: Lipschitz Constant

For a function f:X→Rf:\X\to\RRf:X→R on a metric space (X,d)(\X,d)(X,d), its Lipschitz constant is

Lip⁡(f):=sup⁡x≠y∣f(x)−f(y)∣d(x,y).\Lip(f) \eqdef \sup_{x\ne y} \frac{|f(x)-f(y)|}{d(x,y)}.Lip(f):=x=ysup​d(x,y)∣f(x)−f(y)∣​.
(74)

The function is 1-Lipschitz when Lip⁡(f)≤1\Lip(f)\le1Lip(f)≤1.

Proposition: ccc-Transforms and 1-Lipschitz Functions

Suppose X=Y\X=\YX=Y and c(x,y)=d(x,y)c(x,y)=d(x,y)c(x,y)=d(x,y). Then there exists ggg such that f=gcf=g^cf=gc if and only if Lip⁡(f)≤1\Lip(f)\le1Lip(f)≤1. Furthermore, if Lip⁡(f)≤1\Lip(f)\le1Lip(f)≤1, then fc=−ff^c=-ffc=−f.

Proof

First suppose f=gcf=g^cf=gc for some ggg. For x,y∈Xx,y\in\Xx,y∈X,

∣f(x)−f(y)∣=∣inf⁡z[d(x,z)−g(z)]−inf⁡z[d(y,z)−g(z)]∣≤sup⁡z∣d(x,z)−d(y,z)∣≤d(x,y),|f(x)-f(y)| = \left| \inf_z [d(x,z)-g(z)] - \inf_z [d(y,z)-g(z)] \right| \le \sup_z |d(x,z)-d(y,z)| \le d(x,y),∣f(x)−f(y)∣=∣∣​zinf​[d(x,z)−g(z)]−zinf​[d(y,z)−g(z)]∣∣​≤zsup​∣d(x,z)−d(y,z)∣≤d(x,y),
(75)

where the last inequality is the reverse triangle inequality. Thus Lip⁡(f)≤1\Lip(f)\le1Lip(f)≤1.

If Lip⁡(f)≤1\Lip(f)\le1Lip(f)≤1, then f(x)≤f(y)+d(x,y)f(x)\le f(y)+d(x,y)f(x)≤f(y)+d(x,y), so d(x,y)−f(x)≥−f(y)d(x,y)-f(x)\ge -f(y)d(x,y)−f(x)≥−f(y) for all xxx, hence fc(y)≥−f(y)f^c(y)\ge -f(y)fc(y)≥−f(y). Taking x=yx=yx=y gives fc(y)≤−f(y)f^c(y)\le -f(y)fc(y)≤−f(y). Therefore fc=−ff^c=-ffc=−f. Applying the same property to −f-f−f gives (−f)c=f(-f)^c=f(−f)c=f, so every 1-Lipschitz function is ccc-concave.

By the preceding proposition, a closed dual pair has the form (f,−f)(f,-f)(f,−f) with Lip⁡(f)≤1\Lip(f)\le1Lip(f)≤1. The Kantorovich dual therefore becomes the Kantorovich--Rubinstein formula

W1(α,β)=max⁡f{∫Xf  d(α−β):Lip⁡(f)≤1}=:∥α−β∥W1.\Wass_1(\alpha,\beta) = \max_f \left\{ \int_\X f\,\d(\alpha-\beta) : \Lip(f)\le1 \right\} =: \norm{\alpha-\beta}_{W_1}.W1​(α,β)=fmax​{∫X​fd(α−β):Lip(f)≤1}=:∥α−β∥W1​​.
(76)

This expression depends only on the signed measure ξ=α−β\xi=\alpha-\betaξ=α−β. On compact X\XX, the same supremum defines the Kantorovich--Rubinstein norm on finite signed measures with zero mass Kantorovich & Rubinstein, 1958. Homogeneity and the triangle inequality are immediate, while definiteness follows because Lipschitz functions separate finite Radon measures. On a noncompact pointed space, one uses normalized Lipschitz functions and measures with finite first moment.

For a discrete signed measure α−β=∑krkδzk\alpha-\beta=\sum_k r_k\delta_{z_k}α−β=∑k​rk​δzk​​ with ∑krk=0\sum_k r_k=0∑k​rk​=0,

W1(α,β)=max⁡(fk)k{∑kfkrk:∣fk−fℓ∣≤d(zk,zℓ)for all k,ℓ}.\Wass_1(\alpha,\beta) = \max_{(f_k)_k} \left\{ \sum_k f_k r_k : |f_k-f_\ell|\le d(z_k,z_\ell) \quad\text{for all }k,\ell \right\}.W1​(α,β)=(fk​)k​max​{k∑​fk​rk​:∣fk​−fℓ​∣≤d(zk​,zℓ​)for all k,ℓ}.
(77)

This finite-dimensional linear program can be solved by generic interior-point or first-order methods. If NNN support points are involved, however, it still contains O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) Lipschitz constraints, mirroring the O(nm)O(nm)O(nm) coupling variables of the original discrete Kantorovich LP; the dual formulation alone does not remove the all-pairs structure. The gain comes on structured metric spaces where the distance is generated locally: it is then enough to impose Lipschitz inequalities on neighboring pairs, because summing along paths recovers the constraints between arbitrary points. The one-dimensional ordered case is the first example; the graph-geodesic case is described later in Proposition Proposition: W1\Wass_1W1​ and Beckmann Flow on a Graph.

When d(x,y)=∣x−y∣d(x,y)=|x-y|d(x,y)=∣x−y∣ on R\RRR, ordering the support points z1≤z2≤⋯z_1\le z_2\le\cdotsz1​≤z2​≤⋯ reduces the constraints to neighboring pairs:

W1(α,β)=max⁡(fk)k{∑kfkrk:∣fk+1−fk∣≤zk+1−zkfor all k}.\Wass_1(\alpha,\beta) = \max_{(f_k)_k} \left\{ \sum_k f_k r_k : |f_{k+1}-f_k|\le z_{k+1}-z_k \quad\text{for all }k \right\}.W1​(α,β)=(fk​)k​max​{k∑​fk​rk​:∣fk+1​−fk​∣≤zk+1​−zk​for all k}.
(78)

In one dimension this is equivalent to the cumulative formula given in the one-dimensional transport section.

Wasserstein-1 on Euclidean Spaces¶

In Euclidean space, the Lipschitz constraint has a local differential form and its dual variable is a flux. Let α,β\alpha,\betaα,β have finite first moments and set ξ=α−β\xi=\alpha-\betaξ=α−β. Rademacher’s theorem gives

W1(α,β)=sup⁡f∈Wloc1,∞(Rd){∫Rdf  dξ:∥∇f∥L∞≤1}.\Wass_1(\alpha,\beta) = \sup_{f\in W_{\mathrm{loc}}^{1,\infty}(\RR^d)} \left\{ \int_{\RR^d} f\,\d\xi : \norm{\nabla f}_{L^\infty}\le1 \right\}.W1​(α,β)=f∈Wloc1,∞​(Rd)sup​{∫Rd​fdξ:∥∇f∥L∞​≤1}.
(79)

The flux need not have a Lebesgue density: Dirac-to-Dirac transport already produces a measure concentrated on a segment. Let m∈M(Rd;Rd)m\in\mathcal M(\RR^d;\RR^d)m∈M(Rd;Rd) be a vector-valued Radon measure, let ∣m∣|m|∣m∣ denote its total variation, and define ⟨div⁡m,φ⟩=−∫⟨∇φ, dm⟩\langle\operatorname{div}m,\varphi\rangle=-\int\langle\nabla\varphi,\d m\rangle⟨divm,φ⟩=−∫⟨∇φ,dm⟩.

Proposition: Euclidean Beckmann Formula
W1(α,β)=min⁡m∈M(Rd;Rd){∣m∣(Rd):div⁡(m)=α−β},\Wass_1(\alpha,\beta) = \min_{m\in\mathcal M(\RR^d;\RR^d)} \left\{ |m|(\RR^d) : \operatorname{div}(m)=\alpha-\beta \right\},W1​(α,β)=m∈M(Rd;Rd)min​{∣m∣(Rd):div(m)=α−β},
(80)
Proof

For every feasible mmm and smooth 1-Lipschitz fff, ∫f  d(α−β)=−∫⟨∇f, dm⟩≤∣m∣(Rd)\int f\,\d(\alpha-\beta)=-\int\langle\nabla f,\d m\rangle\le|m|(\RR^d)∫fd(α−β)=−∫⟨∇f,dm⟩≤∣m∣(Rd). The Lipschitz dual gives one inequality. Conversely, if π\piπ is an optimal plan, define

∫⟨ζ, dm⟩=∫ ⁣∫01⟨ζ((1−t)x+ty),y−x⟩ dt  dπ(x,y).\int\langle\zeta,\d m\rangle = \int\!\int_0^1 \left\langle\zeta((1-t)x+ty),y-x\right\rangle \d t\,\d\pi(x,y).∫⟨ζ,dm⟩=∫∫01​⟨ζ((1−t)x+ty),y−x⟩dtdπ(x,y).
(81)

The fundamental theorem of calculus gives div⁡m=α−β\operatorname{div}m=\alpha-\betadivm=α−β, and ∣m∣(Rd)≤∫∥x−y∥  dπ=W1(α,β)|m|(\RR^d)\le\int\norm{x-y}\,\d\pi=\Wass_1(\alpha,\beta)∣m∣(Rd)≤∫∥x−y∥dπ=W1​(α,β).

This is the Beckmann formulation Beckmann, 1952Santambrogio, 2015. If m=w  dxm=w\,\d xm=wdx, its cost is ∫∥w(x)∥  dx\int\norm{w(x)}\,\d x∫∥w(x)∥dx. Outside the source and target mass, div⁡m=0\operatorname{div}m=0divm=0, expressing local conservation.

Once discretized with finite elements, the dual Lipschitz problem and the Beckmann problem become nonsmooth convex optimization problems. The same formulation extends to complete Riemannian manifolds by replacing straight segments with minimizing geodesics and using tangent-valued Radon measures.

Graph Distances and Beckmann Flows¶

Finite graphs give a simple discrete instance where a metric is generated by local moves, so the all-pairs Lipschitz constraints collapse to edge constraints.

Definition: Graph Geodesic Distance

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a connected finite graph with positive edge lengths (ℓe)e∈E(\ell_e)_{e\in E}(ℓe​)e∈E​. The graph geodesic distance between two vertices is

dG(i,j)=min⁡γ:i⇝j∑e∈γℓe.d_G(i,j) = \min_{\gamma:i\leadsto j} \sum_{e\in\gamma}\ell_e .dG​(i,j)=γ:i⇝jmin​e∈γ∑​ℓe​.
(82)

The minimum is over all paths γ\gammaγ joining iii to jjj.

This graph distance turns W1\Wass_1W1​ into a finite-dimensional flow problem.

Proposition: W1\Wass_1W1​ and Beckmann Flow on a Graph

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a connected finite graph with positive edge lengths (ℓe)e∈E(\ell_e)_{e\in E}(ℓe​)e∈E​ and graph geodesic distance dGd_GdG​. For probability vectors a,ba,ba,b on VVV, set r=a−br=a-br=a−b and orient each edge e=(i,j)e=(i,j)e=(i,j). If

(∇Gf)e=fj−fi,div⁡G=−∇G∗(\nabla_G f)_e=f_j-f_i, \qquad \operatorname{div}_G=-\nabla_G^*(∇G​f)e​=fj​−fi​,divG​=−∇G∗​
(83)

are the finite-difference gradient and negative adjoint, then

W1,G(a,b)=max⁡f{∑i∈Vfiri:∣fi−fj∣≤ℓe∀e=(i,j)}=min⁡m{∑e∈Eℓe∣me∣:div⁡Gm=r}.\Wass_{1,G}(a,b) = \max_f \left\{ \sum_{i\in V} f_i r_i : |f_i-f_j|\le\ell_e \quad\forall e=(i,j) \right\} = \min_m \left\{ \sum_{e\in E}\ell_e |m_e| : \operatorname{div}_G m=r \right\}.W1,G​(a,b)=fmax​{i∈V∑​fi​ri​:∣fi​−fj​∣≤ℓe​∀e=(i,j)}=mmin​{e∈E∑​ℓe​∣me​∣:divG​m=r}.
(84)

The vector mem_eme​ is an oriented edge flow, and the constraint div⁡Gm=r\operatorname{div}_G m=rdivG​m=r is conservation of mass at each vertex.

Proof

The edge constraints imply the all-pairs bound by summing along paths and minimizing over paths. Conversely, a 1-Lipschitz function for dGd_GdG​ satisfies ∣fi−fj∣≤dG(i,j)≤ℓe|f_i-f_j|\le d_G(i,j)\le\ell_e∣fi​−fj​∣≤dG​(i,j)≤ℓe​ on every edge. The first equality is therefore the Kantorovich--Rubinstein formula on the metric space (V,dG)(V,d_G)(V,dG​).

For the second equality, write the graph Beckmann problem and dualize its equality constraint with a potential fff:

inf⁡m∑eℓe∣me∣+sup⁡f∑ifi(ri−(div⁡Gm)i).\inf_m \sum_e \ell_e|m_e| + \sup_f \sum_i f_i \left(r_i-(\operatorname{div}_G m)_i\right).minf​e∑​ℓe​∣me​∣+fsup​i∑​fi​(ri​−(divG​m)i​).
(85)

Using div⁡G=−∇G∗\operatorname{div}_G=-\nabla_G^*divG​=−∇G∗​, the coupling term is ∑eme(∇Gf)e\sum_e m_e(\nabla_G f)_e∑e​me​(∇G​f)e​. The minimization over each scalar flow mem_eme​ is finite exactly when ∣(∇Gf)e∣≤ℓe|(\nabla_G f)_e|\le\ell_e∣(∇G​f)e​∣≤ℓe​, and is then equal to zero. The dual problem is the graph Lipschitz dual above. Strong duality holds because this is a finite-dimensional linear program with a nonempty feasible set: connectedness and ∑iri=0\sum_i r_i=0∑i​ri​=0 allow the signed surplus to be routed along paths.

Remark: Sparse LP and Network Simplex

Let N=∣V∣N=|V|N=∣V∣ and M=∣E∣M=|E|M=∣E∣. Writing m=m+−m−m=m^+-m^-m=m+−m− turns graph Beckmann transport into

min⁡m+,m−≥0∑e∈Eℓe(me++me−)subject todiv⁡G(m+−m−)=r.\min_{m^+,m^-\geq0}\sum_{e\in E}\ell_e(m^+_e+m^-_e) \quad\text{subject to}\quad \operatorname{div}_G(m^+-m^-)=r .m+,m−≥0min​e∈E∑​ℓe​(me+​+me−​)subject todivG​(m+−m−)=r.
(86)

This LP has 2M2M2M nonnegative variables and N−1N-1N−1 independent balance constraints, versus N2N^2N2 variables and 2N−12N-12N−1 independent constraints for the dense transport LP. On a sparse graph, M=O(N)M=O(N)M=O(N).

Equivalently, replace each undirected edge by two directed arcs. The result is a minimum-cost transshipment problem to which the network simplex applies: a basis is a spanning tree, and a pivot inserts a non-tree arc and routes flow around the resulting cycle Bertsekas & Eckstein, 1988Orlin, 1997. A basic implementation costs O(PM)O(PM)O(PM) for PPP pivots on a sparse graph. Although PPP depends on the pivot rule, polynomial minimum-cost-flow algorithms are available, and the edge formulation is usually far smaller than the dense transport LP.

This graph formulation is the transshipment version of W1\Wass_1W1​. It is the natural discrete analogue of the Beckmann formulation: gradients are edge differences, divergences are incidence-matrix balances, and geodesic distance is shortest-path length. It can be solved by min-cost flow methods on sparse graphs, while entropic or KL-projection variants lead to flow-Sinkhorn algorithms for graph W1\Wass_1W1​ Beckmann, 1952Peyré, 2026.
